conceptTag: How should a taxi company respond?
readerTitle: A ride app is taking your riders. What kind of threat is it?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (택시 회사, 바닷가 호텔) + 실제 연구 (Christensen 외, HBR 2015의 Uber 분석) · 적용 레슨
insight: 신규 경쟁자에 대응하기 전에, 그 위협이 주류 고객을 정면으로 노리는지 아래에서 올라오는지부터 진단한다. 진단에 따라 정답 대응이 반대로 바뀐다.
misconception: 새로운 앱이나 플랫폼이 기존 업계를 흔들면 모두 '파괴적 혁신'이고, 대응법도 한 가지다.

sources.text: Christensen, C. M., Raynor, M. E., & McDonald, R. (2015). What Is Disruptive Innovation? Harvard Business Review, December 2015.
택시 회사와 호텔 상황은 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Christensen 외(2015)가 Uber는 이론상 파괴적 혁신에 해당하지 않는다고 주장한 내용(로우엔드나 비소비자에서 시작하지 않았고, 기존 고객이 더 낫다고 여긴 서비스로 시작했다)을 원문에서 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 출시 도시나 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.
택시 회사와 호텔 사례는 가상입니다. 실제 업체, 플랫폼 이름, 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Friday night, light rain, two taxis waiting
body: Outside a busy restaurant, four people stand under the awning with their phones out. Across the street, two taxis wait at the rank. Nobody walks over.
The taxi company's owner sees this every weekend now. Fighting back is a given. The harder question comes first: **what kind of threat is this?**

image.label: Diners on phones ignoring taxis across the street
image.brief: 비 오는 밤 식당 차양 아래 휴대폰을 든 손님 네 명, 길 건너 택시 승강장에 빈 택시 두 대. 손님들의 시선은 모두 화면에. 실제 앱 화면, 택시 회사 로고, 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Diagnose the threat first.
body: You own a 60-car taxi firm. A ride app arrived a year ago, and phone bookings have dropped. The riders leaving are your regulars: commuters, diners, airport trips.
They say the app is easier. They can book in seconds, watch the car arrive and see the fare upfront. Which describes the threat best?

options.text: A cheap, worse service for riders you never wanted
options.feedback: That's the shape of low-end disruption. Here, though, your best customers call the app better, not cheaper and worse. Treat it as a low-end threat and you'll ignore it while your core riders leave.

options.text: A better offer aimed straight at your mainstream riders
options.feedback: Yes. This works like a sustaining attack: it wins on what your current customers already value. That calls for a head-on response, and soon.

options.text: A new market of people who never took taxis
options.feedback: The app may pull in some new riders. But the riders you're losing are yours, so new-market disruption doesn't explain your problem.

cards.title: Even Christensen said this wasn't classic disruption.
body: In a 2015 Harvard Business Review article, Clayton Christensen and two co-authors looked at Uber. They argued that by the theory's own definition, it was **not a disruptive innovation**.
It didn't start at the low end, and it didn't start with people who never used taxis. It started with a service that many existing taxi customers found better.
Their point wasn't that taxis were safe. It was that the label changes the right response.

cards.title: Two kinds of threat, two kinds of answer
body: **Sustaining vs disruptive change:** a sustaining rival competes for your customers on the things they already value. A disruptive rival starts with a worse product for customers you overlook, then improves.
Against a sustaining threat, you race head-on and fast. Against a disruptive one, matching features head-on often fails, and a separate, cheaper offer works better.

image.label: Two arrows: one aimed at the core, one rising from below
image.brief: 두 갈래 다이어그램. 왼쪽: 화살표가 가운데 'Your core customers' 원을 정면으로 겨냥, 라벨 'Sustaining: race head-on'. 오른쪽: 화살표가 아래 'Overlooked customers'에서 시작해 위로 휘어 올라감, 라벨 'Disruptive: build a separate offer'. 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: A software company faces the same split. A rival with a cleaner version of your product, sold to your customers, is a race to fix gaps. A free, simpler tool for teams too small to buy from you is the slower, disruptive kind.

cards.title: So how does the taxi firm fight back?
body: You've decided this is a head-on threat to your core riders. You have a fixed budget for one big move this year.

options.text: Close the gaps riders named: app booking, live tracking, upfront fares, card payment
options.feedback: This matches a sustaining threat on its own terms, and you keep your strengths, like ranks and corporate accounts. It costs money and won't guarantee a win, but it fixes the actual reasons people left.

options.text: Cut fares by a quarter to win riders back
options.feedback: Riders didn't leave over price, so a cut gives away margin without fixing booking or tracking. It can also start a price war against a rival with deeper pockets.

options.text: Keep doing what works and wait for rules to catch up
options.feedback: It saves money today. But against a sustaining threat, every month of waiting is another month your regulars form a new habit.

cards.title: The innovator's dilemma, turned around
body: **The innovator's dilemma** says good companies lose by listening to their best customers and ignoring a weak newcomer. Here, your best customers are the ones walking away. Listening to them is exactly right.

The dilemma still holds a warning. The habits that made you good at the old way, like radio dispatch and cash fares, are the ones you'll most want to protect. Ask whether each habit still serves riders, or only serves your routine.

cards.title: A label is a starting point, not a forecast.
body: Getting the diagnosis right doesn't mean you win. The rival may have more money or more drivers. Matching its features may cost more than your margins allow.
Threats also change shape. A rival that starts head-on can later add a cheaper option aimed below you. So check which customers leave, and why, every quarter. Don't settle it once.

cards.title: Now it's a seaside hotel.
body: Your family hotel has 30 rooms, breakfast and a front desk. Home-rental platforms now list cheap rooms in local flats, with no desk and no breakfast.
Backpackers and big budget groups have moved there. Your couples and business guests haven't. What do you do?

options.text: Cut room prices to win back budget guests
options.feedback: This is low-end disruption: the newcomer is cheap because it skips costs you carry. Fighting on price means fighting on its terms, with your costs.

options.text: Ignore the platforms. They serve a different crowd
options.feedback: True for now, and your core guests are safe today. But the innovator's dilemma warns that cheap rivals improve and climb toward your best customers.

options.text: Invest in what core guests value, and test a few self-check-in rooms on the platforms yourself
options.feedback: You defend the core and learn the low end through a small, separate offer. That's the classic answer to a disruptive threat.

cards.softwareNote: The software version: keep improving for paying customers, and run a separate free or lite tier with its own team, so the main product's habits don't smother it.

cards.title: Diagnose the threat before you choose the fight.
body: You used **sustaining vs disruptive change** to read the ride app and the home rentals, **low-end disruption** to spot the hotel's cheap rival, and **the innovator's dilemma** to know when to listen to your best customers and when that can mislead you.
**Try it today:** name your newest competitor. Write down which of your customers it wins and whether they call it better or just cheaper.
